title: New York Suspends Giuliani’s Law License Over False Election Statements
description_medium: In June 2021, New York’s Appellate Division suspended Rudy Giuliani from practicing law on an interim basis. The court found uncontroverted evidence that he made false and misleading statements to courts, lawmakers and the public while challenging the 2020 election. It addressed claims about vote counting and alleged illegal ballots in Georgia and Arizona. The order was an interim disciplinary measure, not a criminal conviction or final disbarment.
description_long: New York’s Appellate Division, First Department, suspended Giuliani from practicing law on June 24, 2021, while an attorney-discipline investigation continued. The court said the disciplinary committee had presented uncontroverted evidence that he made false and misleading statements about the 2020 election to courts, lawmakers and the public. Its opinion examined claims about Georgia’s vote count, supposed underage and deceased voters, and surveillance footage that Giuliani described as showing illegal ballot handling. The court concluded that several statements were false and violated professional-conduct rules, and that the conduct threatened the public interest. The suspension was interim: the court noted that Giuliani remained entitled to a post-suspension hearing and that a later proceeding would determine any final discipline. This ruling therefore supports a specific account of New York’s professional-discipline action, not a claim that courts collectively ruled every election lawsuit frivolous or that Giuliani had already been disbarred.
evidence_notes: The New York Appellate Division’s 2021 opinion directly supports an interim license suspension and its stated basis. It identifies repeated false or misleading election statements; it does not support the frozen title’s sweeping reference to courts ruling Jan. 6 claims frivolous or imply a final disbarment.

title: Peter Navarro Indicted for Contempt of Congress Over Jan. 6 Subpoena
description_medium: On June 3, 2022, federal prosecutors announced Peter Navarro’s indictment on two contempt-of-Congress counts after he refused to comply with a subpoena from the House January 6 committee. The committee sought testimony and documents about his knowledge of events relevant to its Capitol attack investigation. A jury convicted Navarro on both counts in September 2023, and a judge sentenced him to four months in prison in January 2024.
description_long: Former Trump trade adviser Peter Navarro was charged with two counts of contempt of Congress after refusing to comply with a subpoena from the House Select Committee investigating the January 6 attack. The committee ordered him to produce documents and appear for a deposition in February and March 2022. Federal prosecutors announced the indictment on June 3, 2022. Navarro said he was asserting executive privilege at Trump’s direction, but the government prosecuted his failure to appear and provide records under the contempt statute. A federal jury found him guilty of both counts in September 2023. In January 2024, the court imposed four months in prison on each count, to be served concurrently, and a $9,500 fine. The case established criminal consequences for his refusal to answer the committee’s subpoena; it did not decide the committee’s broader conclusions about the Capitol attack or prove that Navarro himself organized the attack.
evidence_notes: DOJ’s indictment, conviction, and sentencing announcements support the charge, subpoena demands, verdict, and sentence. Replaced the unrelated Trump-indictment source with same-case DOJ releases.

title: Trump Becomes First Former U.S. President With a Mug Shot
description_medium: Donald Trump surrendered at Atlanta’s Fulton County Jail on August 24, 2023, for booking in the Georgia election-interference case. Authorities took and released his booking photograph, the first mug shot of a former U.S. president. The booking followed an indictment accusing Trump and allies of conspiring to overturn Georgia’s 2020 election result. His campaign quickly used the image on fundraising merchandise, turning a routine criminal-processing step into a campaign symbol.
description_long: On August 24, 2023, Trump voluntarily surrendered at the Fulton County Jail in Atlanta to be booked on Georgia charges alleging a conspiracy to overturn the state’s 2020 election result. Authorities fingerprinted him, photographed him and released the booking image publicly. The photograph was unprecedented for a former U.S. president: officials had not taken mug shots during his earlier criminal bookings. The image spread widely, and Trump’s campaign soon sold merchandise featuring it and used it in fundraising appeals. The moment joined an ordinary step in criminal processing to the politics of the 2024 campaign. Trump had to post a $200,000 bond and was subject to conditions restricting contact with witnesses and co-defendants and threatening communications. These were pretrial conditions attached to the case, not findings of guilt. The booking image documented that Trump had been processed on the indictment; it did not establish the truth of the allegations, which remained for the courts to decide.
evidence_notes: Washington Post’s August 24 report supports surrender, booking, release of the photo, and bond conditions; its August 25 report supports campaign merchandise using the actual mug shot. Corrected 'President' to 'Former U.S. President' for precision.

title: Sidney Powell Pleads Guilty in Georgia RICO Case
description_medium: On October 19, 2023, attorney Sidney Powell pleaded guilty to six misdemeanor counts of conspiring to interfere with Georgia election duties in the case over efforts to overturn the 2020 result. Her plea concerned an alleged Coffee County scheme to access and copy election data. Powell received six years’ probation, a $6,000 fine and $2,700 in restitution, and agreed to provide documents and testify truthfully in proceedings against co-defendants.
description_long: Sidney Powell, a former Trump campaign lawyer, pleaded guilty on October 19, 2023, in the Georgia prosecution over efforts to reverse the state’s 2020 election result. She admitted six misdemeanor counts of conspiracy to commit intentional interference with the performance of election duties. The plea covered the Coffee County episode: Powell agreed she had paid employees of a forensic firm to travel to the county and copy voter data without authorization, interfering with the election director’s work. The judge sentenced her to six years of probation. Her agreement also required a $6,000 fine, $2,700 in restitution to Georgia, document production and truthful testimony in co-defendants’ trials. Powell’s agreement came one day before jury selection was due to begin, making her the second defendant to plead guilty in the case. The record should be described as a negotiated plea with specific admitted conduct and cooperation terms; it did not itself establish the guilt of the remaining defendants or prove a broader “fake electors” scheme.
evidence_notes: The Washington Post’s same-day report supports the six misdemeanor pleas, Coffee County conduct, probation, fine, restitution, document production, and truthful-testimony agreement. Corrected the malformed fine amount and removed the unsupported implication that the plea concerned a fake-electors scheme.

title: Merchan Restricts Trump’s Public Use of Evidence in Hush-Money Case
description_medium: On May 8, 2023, New York Judge Juan Merchan issued a protective order governing evidence prosecutors would disclose to Donald Trump’s defense in the Manhattan hush-money case. It limited Trump’s public use of discovery materials, including posting them on social media without court approval. The order addressed handling of case evidence; it was distinct from the broader gag order later imposed on statements about witnesses and court personnel.
description_long: Judge Juan Merchan entered a protective order on May 8, 2023, in the Manhattan criminal case charging Donald Trump with falsifying business records. The order governed material turned over by prosecutors during discovery and restricted the defense’s ability to publicize that evidence. In particular, Trump could not post discovery materials on social media without prior court approval. Prosecutors had sought limits to keep discovery within the defense process, while Trump objected that the proposed restrictions burdened his speech. The order was a rule for handling evidence, not a general ban on discussing the prosecution. It also should not be confused with Merchan’s separate, limited gag order in 2024, which restricted public statements about witnesses, prospective jurors and court staff. Keeping those measures distinct clarifies what the May 2023 ruling did: it controlled dissemination of evidence before trial rather than silencing all criticism of the case.
evidence_notes: The linked NBC article is the same-event source but was not readable in the source pass; ABC’s timeline and Lawfare’s review independently document the May 8 order and its restriction on public sharing of discovery. Clarified that this protective order was different from the 2024 gag order.
